Reprisal

rih-PRY-zul · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Reprisal is an act of retaliation, often for harm previously suffered.

The border skirmish quickly escalated as each side launched a reprisal for the other's earlier raid.

Worked Example

After the coach benched him unfairly, some fans worried the star player might quit in reprisal, though he chose to stay and prove himself instead.

A reprisal is an action taken specifically to pay back harm done to you -- it's retaliation, not just a reaction.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

retaliation: Retaliation is the general word for striking back at someone who has harmed you, in any form and on any scale. A reprisal is one specific act of retaliation -- a raid answered with a raid, a punishment answering a punishment. Every reprisal is retaliation, but retaliation names the whole pattern of hitting back.

payback: Payback is the casual, everyday word for getting even -- a prank answered with a prank, one act settling one score. Reprisal is the graver, formal word reporters and historians reach for when the answer to harm is serious: a raid, sanctions, layoffs. Payback fits the playground; reprisal fits the front page.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

forgiveness: the act of letting go of anger over a wrong

goodwill: a friendly, generous attitude toward others

Where it sits · how far the payback actually goes — grudge → reprisal → vendetta

grudge vs. reprisal: A grudge is resentment that just sits and simmers -- a person can hold one for years without acting on it, while a reprisal is the moment someone actually strikes back.

vendetta vs. reprisal: A vendetta is a prolonged, often violent campaign of revenge, far more extreme and sustained than a single reprisal.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: back (Latin)

root — pris-

root — pris-: to seize, to take (from Latin prehendere, by way of French prise, 'a taking')

suffix — -al

suffix — -al: the act of; forms a noun (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Reprisal is built from re- ('back') + pris- ('to seize, to take,' from Latin prehendere, by way of French prise, 'a taking') + -al (a noun ending) -- historically, a reprisal meant seizing something back in return for a loss, which is why the word still carries that sense of a direct payback.

Word Choice

Reprisal almost always implies retaliation for a specific earlier harm -- it's rarely used for a random or unprovoked act. Compare it with the broader requital, which can describe a reward as easily as a punishment.
